span: INHERENT JURISDICTION OF THE HIGH COURT UNDER SECTION 482, Cr.P.C
why: A section heading only; no content to judge.

span: FIR and charge-sheet are liable to be quashed – High Court erred in dismissing the petition under s. 482 Cr.P.C.
why: Headnote holding: the power under s.482 extends to quashing an FIR even after charge-sheet and the High Court should have quashed it.

span: the general rule that normally in exercise of powers under Section 482 Cr.P.C. the criminal proceedings/FIR should not be quashed
why: Headnote states that quashing is the exception to a general rule against it, with exceptions carved out in Bhajan Lal; the case itself goes on to find no exception applies.

span: can even be exercised to quash criminal proceedings relating to non- compoundable offences
why: Court affirms the wide inherent power to quash, including on compromise, though the next paragraph excludes heinous offences from compromise-based quashing.

span: the power under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C. has to be exercised sparingly, carefully and with caution
why: Describes the standard for the power: it exists in three circumstances but is used sparingly; no application to quashing an FIR shown in the passage.

span: Whether a Judge of the High Court can exercise powers under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (for short ‘CrPC’) to alter the sentence
why: Issue concerns altering a sentence, not quashing an FIR.
